prompt: A Ferris wheel of radius $30$ m has its center at the origin. A rider has rotated $150^\circ$ counterclockwise from the rightmost point. What is the rider's exact $x$-coordinate, in meters? For example, type "-12sqrt(3)" for $-12\sqrt{3}$.
hint: On a circle of radius $r$, the coordinates are $(r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta)$ — the unit circle values scaled up by $r$.

hints.text: On a circle of radius $r$, the coordinates are $(r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta)$ — the unit circle values scaled up by $r$.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with radius $4$ at $120^\circ$: $\cos 120^\circ = -\frac{1}{2}$, so $x = 4 \times \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) = -2$. Two steps every time: unit-circle cosine, then multiply by the real radius.

explanation: For a circle of radius $r$, the point at angle $\theta$ is $(r\cos\theta,\ r\sin\theta)$.
$150^\circ$ is in Quadrant II with a $30^\circ$ reference angle, so $\cos 150^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
Multiply by the radius: $x = 30 \times \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -15\sqrt{3}$, about $-26$ m.

alternativeExplanations.title: Does the sign make sense?
steps: After $150^\circ$ the rider is past the top of the wheel and over on the left side.
Left of center means a negative $x$, and $-15\sqrt{3} \approx -26$ m is nearly the full 30 m radius to the left — right for an angle only $30^\circ$ past horizontal.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is $-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$: correct for a unit circle, but this wheel has radius 30, not 1.

Unit-circle values are per-unit-of-radius. Always finish by multiplying by the real radius: $30 \times \left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = -15\sqrt{3}$. A coordinate on a 30 m wheel should be tens of meters, not a fraction under 1.
